Ira taught ethics to second-year students in Bengaluru. She had been watching Jeevan, nineteen, all term.
In class debates, Jeevan argued brilliantly for human dignity above any law. He quoted thinkers, he spoke about rights for everyone.
But in the hostel, she heard, he'd gone along with his group in shutting out a new boy, because "the gang decided".

Ira didn't think Jeevan was a hypocrite. She thought he was nineteen, reasoning differently in different places, like most people.
In the next class, she didn't label anyone. She said, "These stages aren't boxes for people. They're ways of seeing how our reasoning grows, sometimes forward, sometimes back, depending on where we stand."
Jeevan looked up, thoughtful.
